chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Ali, raising it to Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) that he used to say:

O Allah, I and this day are two creations from Your creations. O Allah, do not test me with it, nor test it with me. O Allah, do not let me be seen as audacious in disobeying You, nor as indulging in Your prohibitions. O Allah, turn away from me the doom, the adversities, the afflictions, the evil decrees, the gloating of the enemies, and the evil sight in myself and my wealth.

He said: And there is no servant who says when evening comes and when morning comes, 'I am pleased with Allah as Lord, and with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) as Prophet, and with the Quran as the announcer, and with Ali as Imam' three times, except that it becomes a right upon Allah, the Mighty, the Compeller, to please him on the Day of Judgment.

He said: And he used to say (peace be upon him) when evening comes: 'In the morning we are grateful to Allah, and in the evening we are praising Allah. So for You is the praise just as we came to You in the evening as submitters, safe.'

He said: And when morning comes, he said: 'We have come to the evening as grateful to Allah, and we have come to the morning as praising Allah. And the praise is to Allah just as we came to You in the morning as submitters, safe.'

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Ali ibn Abi Talib)
key_terms.بِالْقُرْآنِ بَلَاغاً: With the Quran as the announcer/messenger
key_terms.رَضِيتُ بِاللَّهِ رَبّاً: I am pleased with Allah as Lord

ai.seo_question: What are the recommended morning and evening supplications in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Kafi highlights the Shia tradition of *Adhkar al-Sha' wa al-Masa'* (morning and evening remembrances), linking daily spiritual discipline to divine protection from *Azl* (calamity) and *Shamatat al-A'da'* (gloating of enemies). The emphasis on reciting satisfaction with the Five Essentials (Allah, Islam, Muhammad, Quran, and Ali) three times reflects the theological centrality of *Imamah* in securing Allah's pleasure, a concept deeply rooted in Shia exegesis of the Verse of Purification and the Verse of Mubahala.
